name: Bokhara
lede: Bokhara is a dark purplish wine red recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, close enough to the already-published Purplish Red that the two articles are each other's nearest listed neighbor.

sections.title: A rare entry, lightly documented
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places Bokhara on plate 47, position L2, and dates its first recorded use to 1925 [1]. The dictionary gives no account of where the name comes from; its origin is undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 lists do not carry the name separately, and the National Bureau of Standards circular cites only Maerz and Paul's entry [1].

The library's measurements place this swatch closest to [[claret-violet|Claret Violet]], 2.6 units off, with [[purplish-red|Purplish Red]], the dark wine red already carried as an article here, close behind at 3.4, and within about 9.7 units of the everyday name [[byzantium|Byzantium]], a brighter, more saturated purple [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a rare painted color: our archive finds a match to this swatch in only 9 of 23,781 paintings, 0.04 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 3 [3]. That makes it rarer than 79 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The small sample is too thin to support a reliable century peak, painter or country figure, so none is claimed here [3].

The earliest match in the archive dates to about 1550, by Jacopo Tintoretto, well over three centuries before the name's 1925 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, not that any pigment or dye matched it, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
